prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which many neutral atoms are trapped at a magic wavelength, bringing frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B012 as a single prize part for Katori and Ye. After the full round-1 exchange the case rests on three points that survived scrutiny. First, the achievement is one distinct idea, state-independent (magic-wavelength) trapping of many neutral atoms, which removes Doppler and recoil shifts and lets stability and accuracy improve together; this is neither the measurement of optical frequencies (2005) nor the control of single trapped ions (2012). Second, the performance, about 1e-18 fractional uncertainty, has been reproduced and compared across independent laboratories on several continents, so it does not depend on one group. Third, it already delivers results: relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants, and a quantitative basis for any redefinition of the second. Seven of eight round-1 files prefer it, but I weigh the independence and consistency of the scientific reasons, not the count. The citation is worded around the lattice concept and its realisation, not around accuracy in general and not around the first demonstration in any single species.
statement.case_against: The residual risks are real. Credit: Takamoto, Hong, Ludlow, Lemke and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups are not named, and I cannot verify the strontium-versus-ytterbium first-demonstration history from the files, so a citation worded around the concept and its realisation is a mitigation, not a resolution. Overlap: the 2005 and 2012 prizes are close neighbours and the committee must be able to say in one sentence why this is not a third metrology prize. Maturity: the redefinition of the second has not happened, though I do not regard it as a condition because the measured performance exists regardless. Finally, I carry a field bias as an atomic physicist, and the conceptual-versus-instrument objection that Eriksson and Mehlig raise for B030 is a legitimate difference of judgment, not one I can dismiss.

responses.point: Eriksson maintains B030 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as his preferred part because a conceptual advance that changed how a class of materials is understood should outrank a precision-measurement advance, lists B012 only as an alternative, and treats the unfinished redefinition of the second as leaving the impact incomplete.
responses.response: I take the conceptual-versus-instrument point seriously, but I do not think B012 is merely an instrument: the magic-wavelength condition is itself a conceptual step, a statement about which atomic states can be trapped without perturbing the transition, and the clock is its demonstration. On B030 I remain where I was, and I think your own attribution paragraph explains why: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe state that Molenkamp tested, and the 3D case (Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents, Hasan and others) is outside three names. A citation naming the HgTe observation makes the trio defensible, as you argue, but it also confines the prize to the 2D case and leaves the prediction credit incomplete, which is a heavier gap than the lattice-clock omissions, where the concept and its first realisation are what we are citing. On timing, a pending metrological decision should not hold up a measured result; if the committee wants B030 later it loses nothing by that, whereas I would not put it ahead of B012 this year.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from B028 to B012 but states that overlap and credit are the strongest reservation, that other lattice-clock pioneers are not covered by two names, and that a citation must show what is new relative to the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I agree that the citation carries the burden and I would put the novelty in its first clause: the optical lattice clock with magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms, as distinct from optical frequency combs and from single-ion control. My proposed wording therefore names the lattice and the many-atom interrogation rather than frequency accuracy as such. On your point that two names may be unfair, I think this is the decisive question for round 2 and I would put it plainly: if the committee could establish that a third person has a claim to the concept comparable to Katori's, I would reopen the allocation; on what the files give me, I cannot establish that, and the supplied attribution of Katori for the concept and Ye for taking accuracy and applications to the frontier is the one I can defend. I also note your caution that low fundamental-theory content should not count in B012's favour, and I do not count it so.

responses.point: Mehlig names the tension between a conceptual discovery (B030) and an instrument achievement as open, and wants the citation to mention relativistic geodesy and tests of fundamental physics, while stressing that lattice-clock credit is shared with Takamoto, Hong, Ludlow and Lemke.
responses.response: I accept part of your wording: mentioning relativistic geodesy and tests of fundamental physics in the citation helps show that this is a physics result and not only a metrology one, and I would be content with such a clause as long as the lead remains the lattice concept. I would not, however, resolve the conceptual-versus-instrument tension by ranking B030 higher, because you and I agree that the BHZ omission is the more serious attribution gap. I would also keep the instrument framing honest: the achievement is the 1e-18 lattice clock as demonstrated, and the citation should not promise a redefinition of the second that the metrology community has not yet decided.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, moved from B042 to B012 and concedes that B042 has the larger recent scientific footprint and that its attribution is less settled than he had assumed.
responses.response: Your concession is consistent with my view, and it is why I keep B042 as my first alternative. My answer to the chair's question is that B042 could become lead if the superconducting mechanism were settled and if the credit among Jarillo-Herrero, Cao, Dean, Young, Efetov and the theorists (MacDonald, Bistritzer, Lopes dos Santos and others) could be fixed within three names; neither is true on the files today, and Olsson's doubt about Bistritzer suggests the allocation is not yet stable. I would not support adding B042 as a second part, because that would force either a fourth person or a split of experimental credit that the three-person limit does not allow.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B012 and argues that credit for early lattice-clock demonstrations can be handled in the citation text rather than in the laureate list, while doubting that Bistritzer belongs with B042.
responses.response: I agree with your handling of credit and I think it answers the chair's first question as far as the committee can answer it: the citation can name the lattice-clock concept and its realisation, which does not claim that Katori and Ye did every first demonstration. I do not think the files let us confirm the strontium-versus-ytterbium history, so I would not treat that as settled; I would ask the secretariat to check it before the vote and, if it shows that someone other than Katori holds the concept, accept that the result could change my position. Your doubt about Bistritzer also reinforces my view that B042 needs another year or two before a three-name allocation is defensible.

uncertainties: Whether the first-demonstration and credit history of lattice clocks (Takamoto, Hong, Ludlow, Lemke, strontium versus ytterbium, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) supports a two-name award; I cannot verify it from the files and my position would be revisited if it showed a comparable claim to the concept.
Whether the committee accepts the citation wording around magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I do not know whether Eriksson is persuaded.
Whether a prize before the redefinition of the second will be read as premature, which I do not think it should be.
Whether the committee prefers a conceptual discovery (B030) or an instrument achievement when support is split; this is a difference of judgment, not a factual question.
Whether B042 will settle on mechanism and credit soon enough to be a lead candidate in a later year.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B012 (Katori, Ye). My documented connections (Svanberg, Aldén, John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, Rippe, Walther, Kinos, WACQT, Deep Light Vision, European quantum-memory collaborations) do not include the candidates, although my stay in Hall's laboratory is in the same broad laser-metrology milieu as JILA, and I declare my field bias as an atomic physicist. My WACQT involvement remains a possible recusal issue for B005 and, more loosely, for B020 and B002, and I do not propose any of them as preferred; B020 appears only as an alternative ballot ID. This disclosure is unchanged from round 1.
